questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Finding wild food to eat, and doing it safely
How to grow mushrooms at home in the dark
Why supermarkets sell less fresh fruit now
Traditional cooking in South Africa
questions.why: They meet two young women who forage for wild food and stress eating only what they can identify.

questions.q: How do Pippa and Beth feel about foraging?
options: They both forage for wild mushrooms often
Pippa loves wild mushrooms, but Beth doesn't
They have never eaten any wild food at all
Both would eat blackberries, but fear mushrooms
questions.why: Pippa picked blackberries but would be nervous about mushrooms; Beth says she's 'exactly the same'.

questions.q: What important rule do both foragers follow?
options: Only pick food early in the morning
Only eat what you can identify for certain
Never eat anything raw, even berries
Always forage in a group of three or more
questions.why: Pippa says they only eat what they can identify with 100% certainty: 'If in doubt leave it out!'

questions.q: How did Roushanna Gray learn to forage?
options: At university, on a plant science course
From books and videos she found online
From her mother-in-law, a plant expert
From local farmers near her home
questions.why: She learned from her mother-in-law, a horticulturalist with a deep knowledge of plants.

questions.q: According to Roushanna, what is incredibly important in foraging?
options: Being completely sure you can eat a plant
Finding the rarest plants in the area
Picking as much as possible each time
Cooking all plants for a long time
questions.why: She says it's incredibly important to know 'a hundred and ten percent' if you can eat it.

questions.q: Why did Emily Smith move to rural Japan?
options: To open a small restaurant in the mountains
To study traditional Japanese cooking
To teach English at a local school
To work on a wild mushroom project
questions.why: Beth says she moved there to work on a project cataloguing and collecting wild mushrooms.

questions.q: How many kinds of mushroom are there in Japan, and how many are edible?
options: About 300, and almost all are edible
About 500, and 30 are edible
About 5,000, and 300 are edible
About 5,000, and none are edible
questions.why: Beth says there are around 5,000 varieties, 300 of which are edible.

questions.q: What does Emily think about people's fear of mushrooms?
options: It is completely right, as mushrooms are the most dangerous food
It is unfair, because plants can be just as dangerous
It is silly, because all mushrooms are safe
It only exists in Japan
questions.why: She says the stigma is misplaced, because plants can be just as dangerous, if not more.
